items.passage: When the night nurse walked home from the ward each dawn, she passed the clock-maker's shop, and Hedwig was always already at his bench, easing the same brass wheel into the same tall clock. Winifred, her patient in bed four, had sent it to him in the spring. Each week Winifred asked the nurse not whether it was mended but whether Hedwig was still at it, and each week the nurse said yes. One morning Hedwig set down his loupe and said the clock would never keep true time again; the case had warped past saving. The nurse carried the news back to the ward like a cold cup of tea. Winifred was ______ when she heard it. She asked that Hedwig be told to keep working all the same, and that night she wound her small wristwatch and held it near her ear until she slept.

items.passage: Cleotilde and Imtiaz had played chess in the abandoned orchard outside Lyon every Sunday since the club lost its hall. __Their board sat on a cut stump, and beneath it, on a card gone soft with damp, the club's oldest rule declared that a piece once touched must be moved.__ The pear trees had gone wild; fruit split in the grass and drew wasps. The two rivals spoke little, played slowly, and kept score in a notebook that neither would let the other hold. For eleven years the lead had passed between them like a coin. This Sunday a wasp settled on Imtiaz's queen. He flicked it off, and his knuckle tipped the queen onto its side. Moving her now would cost him the game and the lead. Cleotilde studied the fallen piece, then the stump. She drew out the card, folded it once, and put it in her coat. Then she stood the queen upright on her square and waited for him to play.

items.passage: When the season ended on Maui, the little theater on Front Street ran one film a night for whoever wandered in, and Bogdan, who had run its projector for thirty years, let Larissa sit with him in the booth. __He called her Lara, as her grandmother had, and she let him, though no one else had used that name since the funeral.__ They watched through the small square window while the reel ticked beside them. Between shows Bogdan oiled the gears and told her which seats squeaked and which ones leaked when it rained. In October he asked her to thread the projector by herself. Her hands shook; twice the film slipped from the sprockets, and twice he said nothing. When the picture at last steadied on the screen, he took a marker from his pocket. On the strip of tape above the booth door, under his own name, he wrote a second one: Lara.

items.passage: Aiko kept everything. In the harbor town in Hokkaido where we had both retired, her house held forty years of programs from the theater where we once sang duets, each pressed flat and labeled by year. __She told me once, over tea, that she had never missed a single performance of mine, not even after we stopped singing together.__ I laughed, and she poured more tea. Her husband, Haruo, mended nets on the jetty below the house and lifted a hand whenever I passed. Last winter, after Aiko's stroke, Haruo asked me to help him sort her desk. In the bottom drawer, beneath the programs, lay ticket stubs, one for every concert I had given alone, in Osaka, in Sendai, in cities she had sworn she had never seen. Haruo held one to the window light. He did not ask what it meant, and I returned the stubs to the order in which she had left them.

items.passage: I keep my spice stall in the old galley of a ship that someone dragged ashore in Marrakesh, and Joaquin has been my worst customer for nine years. He haggles over cumin he has already decided to buy. He tells strangers that my scales lean toward the house. Last spring his nephew in Valencia offered him a room and a job minding a café, and Joaquin announced it to the whole galley as if I had lost a bet. I told him Valencia was finally getting someone to argue with. Hamza, he said, you will starve without my complaints. I was not worried, exactly. Still, I began weighing his cumin a little heavy, which he noticed and called theft in reverse. The week he was meant to leave, I did not take down the card above the stove that reads JOAQUIN'S STOOL, though I had threatened to for years. On the Thursday he came in anyway, his ticket folded in his shirt pocket, and I poured his tea before he finished complaining about the price.

options: Mild relief at his departure while trading jokes about his complaints
Warm regard for him while feeling guilty about his claims of unfair scales
Quiet reluctance to lose him while treating his departure as a joke
Good-natured rivalry with him while expecting the café to suit him better

items.passage:
Three things I carry on the crossing:
her cane, her folding stool, and the rule we never made aloud.
Solange, retired from the bench, walks the dry bed of the river
like a docket, ruling on each stone:
too loose, too proud, inadmissible.
I, Jonah, her clerk, young enough to be her grandson,
take notes on nothing and sigh where she can hear me.
She is slower now. I tell her so. She overrules me.
I am not keeping count, exactly, of the times she stops.
At the bend the bank still wears the high mark of that spring,
and past it, if you know where to look, the courthouse roof.
Lately I point out herons there,
late herons, early herons, herons that turn out to be stumps,
and I set the stool down facing upstream
so that when she rests she has the long bed of stones before her
and nothing at her back but me.

Tired impatience with her while putting up with her rulings out of habit
Deep respect for her while feeling uneasy about his own role in the case
Amused regard for her rulings while keeping careful count of her pauses

items.passage: Diesel and dill: the compartment smelled of both, and of the cucumber sandwiches my father had packed in Krakow as if the train to Przemyśl were crossing a desert. On his knee lay the newspaper with my article, the first I had written in English for a paper anyone in Poland had heard of. He was reading it aloud in Polish to Tatiana, a retired teacher across from us, and improving it as he went; my sentence about bus timetables became something about the dignity of travelers. I corrected him twice. Brigid, he said, a translator is permitted his small liberties. I would not say I minded, exactly. When Tatiana asked for the paper so her grandson could see it, I heard myself tell her it was our only copy, which was true in the sense that I had left the other four in my suitcase. Near Tarnów my father fell asleep with the page under his hand, and I shifted my bag on the rack so the sun stayed off his face and off the print.

items.passage: Three rules governed Miss Kai's workroom on Harbour Street in the year 1861: measure twice, cut once, and say nothing you would not stitch your name to. I was fourteen and her only apprentice, and I broke the third rule weekly. One Sunday on the sea wall at Kingston, watching her pin her old shawl against the wind, I told her that when I had a shop of my own I would make her a proper coat, blue, with horn buttons. She laughed and asked which shop that would be. On the shelf behind her cutting table lay a bolt of blue linen that she dusted each Saturday and never offered to a customer. I left her service at nineteen and did not go back to Harbour Street. Last month, with my own sign over my own door, a carter brought me a parcel in brown paper. Inside were the blue linen, a card of horn buttons, and a slip in her square hand: chest 34, sleeve 22, as of 1861. I have measured the cloth twice.

options: It recounts the rules and Sunday walks that shaped a young apprentice's early training.
It shows that a remark the narrator made lightly was held binding by his teacher.

It suggests that the narrator's later success led his teacher to recall a promise.

items.passage: Receipts curled out of the printer at the all-night pharmacy on Długa Street, and Valentina tore each one off without reading it. A year earlier, the night her brother Suhyun left for his posting, he had borrowed her grey scarf for the bus to the barracks. She sent two messages about it that first month, one a photograph of the empty hook by her door, and then sent nothing more. When their mother asked on the phone whether he ever wrote back, Valentina talked about the weather in Gdańsk instead. The hook stayed empty; her winter coat hung on the doorknob all season. At ten past three one February morning the door chimed, and Suhyun stood by the cough syrups in a coat too thin for the Baltic wind. The scarf was wound twice at his throat, its fringe knotted where it had frayed, one end darned in thread a shade too dark, the work of someone who had practiced on it under a barracks lamp. He set a packet of lozenges on the counter. She slid his coins back across to him.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: It recounts a sister's early efforts to recover a scarf her brother had borrowed.
It depicts a late-night meeting between a pharmacist and her brother back from service.
It suggests that a long silence over a borrowed scarf concealed care on both sides.
It implies that a sister's unanswered messages led her brother to mend the scarf.

items.passage: We met Elisa at the Posillipo pool at seven, before the swim club arrived with its whistles and foam boards. My brother had brought goggles; she put them in her bag. Her method had four steps, which she recited like bus stops: lie back, ears under, hands open, stop helping. Her grandfather had taught it to fishermen's sons on this coast, she said, back when there were fishermen's sons. Now she taught it to my brother on Tuesdays, for less than the club charged for a cap. He sank eleven times. 'Count, Giada,' she said, so I counted from the bench, beside a lemon ice someone had abandoned. On the twelfth try he floated, arms out, eyes on the sky. Elisa did not clap. She slid one palm under the back of his head, not lifting, and kept it there while the swim club filed in, until a coach asked for the lane.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall tone of the text?
options: Wry and quietly reverent toward a method few still pass on
Brisk and comic toward a boy's clumsy first swimming lesson
Relieved and gentle toward a lesson that has finally succeeded
Nostalgic and fond toward the fishing families of the old coast

items.explanation: 앞부분은 고글을 압수하고 방법을 버스 정류장처럼 외는 장면, '어부의 아들들이 있던 시절'이라는 농담조 문장으로 건조하고 재치 있는 겉 어조를 만든다. 중간에 수영 클럽보다 싼 값에 화요일마다 가르친다는 디테일이 사라져 가는 기술을 암시하고, 끝에서 Elisa는 박수 대신 손바닥을 소년의 머리 밑에 받친 채 클럽 사람들이 들어올 때까지 놓지 않는다. 겉의 재치와 속의 경건한 정성이 겹치므로 A가 정답이다. B는 겉 층만, C는 손을 받친 이유를 수업이 끝난 안도로 뒤집었고, D는 대상을 어촌 가족 전체로 넓혔다.

items.passage: Wira drinks his coffee black at the Tutuban station café at twenty to six, before the first run to Cubao, and I drink mine at the next table because that is where I have sat since 1979. Between sips he fixes things. On Tuesday it was the cashier's transistor radio. On Wednesday it was a schoolboy's calculator, opened with a bent fork. On Thursday the waitress brought her mother's wristwatch, and he wound it, listened, nudged something with a pin, and handed it back ticking. Narong, she told me, your friend should open a shop. Everyone says this. The waitress said it again on Friday while refilling his cup at the usual price. That morning his own wrist was bare, a pale band where the strap had been, and he read the time off the café clock. He counted coins onto the saucer twice before he went out to the bus.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall tone of the text?
options: Cheerful and admiring toward a driver's gift for small repairs
Plain and quietly troubled toward skill that is praised but not repaid
Gloomy and pitying toward a driver who has lost his own watch
Detached and scornful toward a café that takes favors freely

items.explanation: 앞부분은 요일별 수리를 짧고 건조하게 나열해 담담한 겉 어조를 만든다. 중간에 웨이트리스가 칭찬을 하면서도 커피는 '평소 가격'으로 채운다는 디테일이 끼어들고, 끝에서 시계 없이 카페 시계를 보고 동전을 두 번 세는 Wira의 동작이 보답 없는 재능에 대한 조용한 불편함을 드러낸다. 두 층을 모두 담은 B가 정답이다. A는 겉의 감탄만 읽었고, C는 불편함의 원인을 시계를 잃은 일로 바꾸었으며, D는 같은 감정을 카페 전체에 대한 경멸로 넓혔다.

items.passage: We split the house in one afternoon. Colby took the kitchen table, I took the barometer, and we tossed a coin for the ladder, which he won and then lent back to me before I had reached the car. The gate was harder to divide. Twelve summers ago we had rebuilt the cemetery gate at St. Elwyn's, my welding and his hinges, or his welding and my hinges, depending on which of us was telling the vicar. The parish newsletter had printed one name, his, and spelled it wrong. Jamal, he said that evening, nobody reads the newsletter. I kept the clipping anyway, in the barometer's case. Driving out of the village we stopped at the gate, and Colby ran a thumb along the top rail and said the hinges still swung true, which was a compliment to whoever had hung them. Before we left, I wedged the clipping into a crack in the post, name side out, facing the headland and the rain.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall tone of the text?
options: Breezy and amused toward the task of dividing a family house
Gracious and humbled toward a brother who lent back the ladder
Wry and quietly conceding toward an old contest over credit
Nostalgic and fond toward the summers spent working on the coast
items.recipeBeyondMedium: 겉 어조만 읽으면 오답에 걸리고 속 어조의 원인까지 맞혀야 하며, 네 선택지 구조가 동일해 형식 단서가 없다
items.explanation: 앞부분은 집을 나누는 과정을 짧게 나열하고 '누가 신부님께 말하느냐에 따라' 같은 농담으로 건조하고 재치 있는 겉 어조를 만든다. 중간에 화자가 철자까지 틀린 신문 스크랩을 기압계 상자에 몰래 보관해 왔다는 디테일이 공로 문제가 남아 있었음을 보여 준다. 끝에서 화자는 그 스크랩을 형의 이름이 보이게 문기둥 틈에 끼워 비바람에 맡기며 다툼을 조용히 내려놓는다. 따라서 C가 정답이며, A는 겉 층만, B는 양보의 원인을 사다리 일로 바꾸었고, D는 대상을 해안의 여름 전체로 넓혔다.

items.passage: Nadeesha, said Father Xiulan, as if he had seen me at Mass the Sunday before and not three years earlier, and because the hall at the Railway Hotel in Galway held more guests than chairs, he put a hymnal in my hands to keep my place at the end of a bench. For the first hour of that June wedding breakfast in 1913 the book was furniture. I fanned myself with it, rested my cup on it, laid my gloves across its cover. We spoke of the bride's lace, the rain, the fare to Dublin. Neither of us spoke of the choir loft at St. Nicholas, where I had sung each Sunday until my brother's funeral. When the fiddlers stopped to drink, he reached across, opened the hymnal to a page with one corner folded down, and turned back to his cake. I closed it. During the toasts I held it on my knee, shut, with one finger inside at that page, and when the guests sat down I did not take the finger out.
items.question: In the text, the hymnal most likely represents
options: the narrator's guarded move back toward the past the two avoid.
a handy object that helps the narrator cope with a crowded room.
the narrator's easy comfort with the polite talk among the guests.
a rift between the narrator and the priest that his gesture mends.
items.recipeBeyondMedium: 사물이 두 맥락에서 다른 의미를 띠고, 가장 강한 오답이 인물 관계로 읽은 그럴듯한 상징 해석이다
items.explanation: 찬송가는 처음에 부채·찻잔 받침·장갑 놓는 곳처럼 도구로만 쓰이며, 두 사람이 성가대 이야기를 피하는 동안 대화는 잡담에 머문다. 신부가 접힌 쪽을 펼치자 화자는 책을 닫지만, 마지막에는 책을 덮은 채 그 쪽에 손가락을 끼워 두고 빼지 않는다. 닫음과 손가락의 대비는 피해 온 과거로 조심스럽게 돌아가려는 움직임을 보여 주므로 A가 정답이다. B는 문자적 기능, C는 앞 맥락의 잡담만 반영했고, D는 두 사람 사이의 불화와 화해로 읽었지만 지문에 다툼의 근거가 없고 마지막 동작은 화자 자신의 과거를 향한다.

items.passage: Folded twice and then once more, Salma's invitation lay on the planks of the dock, weighted with a lemon. Her son's bride had come to Marrakesh only that spring, in the year 1868, and the small lake below the rented villa was the one place in the household where no one followed anyone. The luncheon the card announced was a week off, and the bride had not answered. Each evening she walked to the end of the dock, lifted the lemon, unfolded the card, read the date, and refolded it along the same creases before setting the lemon back. Wolfram, watching from the terrace with his pipe, called the card his mother's little tide. Salma heard him and went on shelling beans. On the third evening the bride carried the lemon up to the kitchen, sliced it, and served it with the tea, and the card stayed on the boards with nothing to hold it but the stillness of the air.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “little tide” most nearly suggests that the invitation is
options: a pressure that keeps rising until the bride is made to yield
a summons that keeps drawing the bride back to an open choice
a deadline that is ebbing away as the luncheon draws near
a message that moves slowly between the two women of the house
items.recipeBeyondMedium: 관용 해석으로 풀 수 없고, 오답이 비유의 다른 속성에서 나온 그럴듯한 해석이며 정답은 두 곳 이상의 단서가 정한다
items.explanation: 비유 앞에서 신부는 일주일 뒤 오찬 초대에 아직 답하지 않았고, 매일 저녁 부두 끝으로 가 카드를 펼쳐 날짜를 읽고 다시 접는 행동을 되풀이한다. 이 두 단서는 '밀물'이 매번 돌아와 신부를 미결정의 선택 앞으로 데려가는 성질을 가리킨다. 비유 뒤에서 레몬을 치워 카드를 바람에 맡기는 장면도 선택이 여전히 열려 있음을 보여 주므로 B가 정답이다. A는 차오르는 압력, C는 빠져나가는 썰물이라는 다른 속성을 골랐고, D는 두 사람 사이를 오가는 전달물로 의미를 넓혔다.

items.passage: When the ice truck stopped calling at the Colombo harbor in 1987, Ayita began packing the morning catch in sawdust from the boatyard. Her family's stall had sold fish on that corner for forty years. Its shutter now stuck halfway each dawn, while the new stalls across the lane rolled theirs up with motors and played radios for the buyers. Faisal, who had fished beside her grandfather, came by every morning, lifted the shutter the last few inches with his shoulder, and left without buying. The customers who still came were old ones, and they paid in exact change. One wet morning, watching a grandmother count out coins, Faisal said the stall was the song a band plays after the dancers have gone home. Ayita wrote it on the back of a receipt. The next week she ordered a new spring for the shutter, and she taped the receipt inside the lid of the cash tin.
items.question: As used in the text, the phrase “the song a band plays after the dancers have gone home” most nearly suggests that the stall is
options: a cheerful sound that still brightens mornings at the harbor
a business drowned out by the radios of newer stalls
a business still serving a loyal few after its time
a custom that the whole harbor is slowly leaving behind
items.recipeBeyondMedium: 관용 해석으로 풀 수 없고, 오답이 비유의 다른 속성에서 나온 그럴듯한 해석이며 정답은 두 곳 이상의 단서가 정한다
items.explanation: 비유 앞에서 얼음 트럭이 끊기고 새 가판대들이 모터와 라디오로 손님을 끄는 반면, 이 가판대에는 나이 든 손님들만 남아 있다. 또 Faisal은 매일 아침 어깨로 셔터를 마저 올려 주며 가게가 계속 열리도록 돕는다. 두 단서를 함께 만족하는 해석은 '때는 지났지만 남은 몇몇을 위해 계속되는 가게'이며, 비유 뒤 새 스프링을 주문하는 장면도 이와 어긋나지 않으므로 C가 정답이다. A는 노래의 즐거운 소리, B는 라디오 표현을 빌린 소음, D는 항구 전체로 범위를 넓힌 해석이다.

items.passage: Istanbul's afternoon wind comes up off the Golden Horn and rattles the paper drying on the lines in the kite-maker's yard behind our building. __The old man dyes his own string and writes every color a customer orders in a ledger he has kept since before I was born.__ Eleni's plan was that the two of us would build a kite for my sixteenth birthday, since my father was working late again. I told her it was a project for children. She said maybe, and paid for the frames. We cut the paper without talking. The kite-maker showed us how to lash the spars, then went in for tea, leaving the ledger open on his bench under a stone. By four the kite was done, red and white, and it climbed on the first try above every other kite in the yard. Eleni let out the line. It was a pale blue I had not seen in years, and on the open page, in faded ink, beside an order from eleven summers ago, was my mother's name. Neither of us said anything. The kite stayed up.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It sets out a detail of the yard before the kite-building begins
It introduces a figure whose craft the narrator then dismisses as childish
It points to how Eleni was able to choose the string's color
It shows the care with which the kite-maker treats his customers
items.recipeBeyondMedium: 밑줄 문장의 기능을 지문 후반 사건이 바꾸므로 밑줄 근처만 읽으면 오답에 걸리고, 오답이 모두 지문에 근거한 기능이다
items.explanation: 밑줄 문장은 단독으로 보면 연 장인의 습관을 소개하는 배경 묘사처럼 보인다. 그러나 중간에 장부가 벤치에 펼쳐져 있다는 장면이 지나가고, 끝에서 Eleni가 고른 연줄이 어머니가 예전에 주문한 하늘색이며 그 장부에 어머니 이름이 있다는 사실이 드러난다. 이 후반 사건 때문에 밑줄 문장은 Eleni가 줄 색을 알아낸 경로를 미리 심어 둔 문장으로 다시 읽히므로 C가 정답이다. A는 밑줄 문장만 본 기능, B는 바로 뒤 화자의 냉소와 연결해 방향을 잘못 읽었고, D는 장인의 정성으로 일반화해 후반 단서를 설명하지 못한다.

items.passage: We waited out the rain at the bus shelter on the hill road above Karachi, my sister Sadia and I, with our mother's letters in a plastic sleeve and the conservatory audition two days off. __Our mother, Ayesha, wrote to us every week of her last year abroad, always in pencil, and always, she said, because pencil could be corrected.__ Sadia was to play the cello for the panel and I was to turn her pages, so we rehearsed under the tin roof, she humming the bars, I flipping pages that were not there. Between passages we read a letter aloud, then another. A bus came and went without us. A goat looked into the shelter and left. When the rain eased, Sadia took the score from her case and opened it to the passage she always stumbled on, and along its margin, under fingerings she had written herself, I saw fainter numbers in another hand, rubbed half out and written again.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It introduces a habit of the mother's that the score's margin later recalls
It describes the letters that the siblings go on to read aloud together
It gives family background that accounts for the siblings' trip to the audition
It suggests that written words can keep an absent parent close at hand
items.recipeBeyondMedium: 밑줄 문장의 기능을 지문 후반 사건이 바꾸므로 밑줄 근처만 읽으면 오답에 걸리고, 오답이 모두 지문에 근거한 기능이다
items.explanation: 밑줄 문장은 단독으로는 어머니의 편지에 관한 가족 배경 설명처럼 보인다. 중간에 남매가 편지를 소리 내어 읽는 장면이 이어지지만, 끝에서 악보 여백에 지웠다가 다시 쓴 다른 사람의 운지 숫자가 발견된다. '고칠 수 있어서 연필로 쓴다'는 어머니의 습관이 이 연필 흔적과 연결되면서 밑줄 문장은 마지막 발견을 미리 준비한 문장으로 바뀌므로 A가 정답이다. B는 바로 뒤 장면과의 관계, C는 표면적 배경 기능만 보았고, D는 편지 표현을 빌려 일반적 주제로 넓혔다.

items.passage: Lamp oil and old glue were what I smelled first each morning in the library in Naples, where I was apprenticed to Milena at nineteen. __Every afternoon she brought me a pastry from the bakery on the corner and set it on my desk without a word.__ I was restless that year, forever asking to work in the reading room instead of the bindery, forever glancing at the door. Milena kept me at the bench, teaching me to resew spines and float torn pages. When I had eaten, she would take the brown wrapper, smooth it flat against her knee, and carry it off to her own desk, which I put down to thrift. In March the roof leaked, and for two weeks we dried map plates on lines strung between shelves. More than once I wondered whether the pastries were apology or bribe. In the spring a collector came to inspect the library's oldest atlas, asking who had sewn the fourth section. Milena opened her drawer and laid out a stack of brown squares, each marked in her small hand with a date and a page.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It establishes Milena's quiet generosity toward an apprentice who is restless and distracted.
It introduces a habit later revealed as Milena's method of tracking the narrator's work.
It sets up the suspicion, voiced later, that Milena used the pastries as a bribe.
It suggests that small kindnesses between people at work can carry several meanings.
items.recipeBeyondMedium: 밑줄 문장의 기능을 지문 후반 사건이 바꾸므로 밑줄 근처만 읽으면 오답에 걸리고, 오답이 모두 지문에 근거한 기능이다
items.explanation: 밑줄 문장은 단독으로 보면 Milena의 친절을 보여 주는 배경 묘사처럼 읽힌다. 그러나 중간에 Milena가 포장지를 펴서 자기 책상으로 가져가는 장면이 나오고, 마지막에 그 포장지마다 날짜와 페이지가 적혀 있었음이 드러나면서 이 습관이 화자의 작업을 기록하는 수단이었음이 밝혀진다. 따라서 B가 정답이다. A는 밑줄 문장만 읽은 표면 해석이고, C는 뇌물 의심을 결론처럼 받아들인 해석이며, D는 지문 표현을 일반론으로 넓혀 후반 사건을 설명하지 못한다.

items.passage: Bergen rain had warped every shelf in the studio by the spring Thorvald came to replace them, and he let me know it was my fault for stacking wet pots too close together. He measured each plank three times and talked to the wood more than to me. I said, often and loudly, that he worked like a glacier. Then my teacher looked at my first glazed bowl and remarked, within Thorvald's hearing, that I threw pots the way a carpenter joins wood: careful, square, and without any joy. I told myself I did not care what either of them thought. That is not quite true, I suppose. For the rest of that month I left the kettle full and warm on the stove when I went home, though I never drink tea after noon. Thorvald finished the shelves in May. I still called him a glacier to the other students, but I began to time my glazing for the afternoons he came back to oil the joints, and I kept the stool by the window clear.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Thorvald?
options: She mocks his slow pace while quietly arranging to spend time near him.
She complains about his slow pace while waiting for the shelves to be finished.
She respects his careful work while hoping to make amends for the wet pots.
She resents the carpenter comparison while trying to work more carefully herself.
items.recipeBeyondMedium: 말투와 행동의 어긋남을 읽어야 하고, 네 선택지가 같은 양가 구조라 형식 단서가 없다
items.explanation: 화자는 앞부분에서 Thorvald를 빙하라고 부르며 불평하지만, 중간에 '그건 완전히 사실은 아니다'라고 스스로 정정한다. 이후 마시지도 않는 차를 위해 주전자를 데워 두고, 선반 작업이 끝난 뒤에도 그가 오는 오후에 맞춰 유약 작업을 하며 창가 의자를 비워 둔다. 따라서 겉으로는 놀리지만 실제로는 그의 곁을 찾는다는 A가 정답이다. B는 말투만 읽었고 작업이 끝난 뒤의 행동을 설명하지 못하며, C는 호감의 이유를 죄책감으로 바꿨고, D는 선생님의 비유를 빌린 일반화다.

items.passage: I was eleven when I carried the rumor home. In the school music room everyone said that Siti, who had taught there since before I was born, would be sent away at the end of term, and I repeated it at dinner because it sounded important. My grandfather put down his spoon and asked me to say it again, slowly. He and Siti had not spoken in twenty years, for reasons no one at our table would name. The next morning he put on his good shirt, the one kept for funerals, and walked toward the school; my mother told the neighbors he had gone to the market. That week the upright piano in the music room stayed locked, and its key hung on a nail no one would touch. By the cool season the story had come to nothing, and Siti stayed. On Saturdays a satchel of sheet music began to appear on our hall bench, and from the kitchen I could hear two old players arguing over tempo, then starting the same bar again. Aung, my grandfather would call, bring the second chair.
items.question: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: A boy repeats a rumor at dinner and sends his grandfather on a hidden errand.
Two old musicians take up playing together again after many years of silence.

### lit40-hard-02-062 — skill words_in_context · 유형 word_in_context
[지문]

[질문] Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
A) calmly accepting
B) visibly stricken
C) stubbornly hopeful
D) mildly relieved

[표시된 정답] A
[해설]
앞부분에서 Winifred는 시계가 고쳐졌는지가 아니라 Hedwig가 아직 작업 중인지를 묻는데, 이는 그녀가 수리의 결과보다 과정에 마음을 두고 있음을 보여 준다. 고칠 수 없다는 말을 들은 뒤에도 그녀는 그래도 계속해 달라고 부탁하고 손목시계를 감아 귀에 댄 채 잠들므로 반응은 동요 없는 수용이다. 따라서 두 조건을 모두 만족하는 A가 정답이다. C는 계속해 달라는 부탁만 보고 고른 근접 표현이지만 그녀는 처음부터 완성을 기대하지 않았고, B는 간호사가 느낀 무거움을 그녀에게 옮겼으며, D는 안도할 이유가 지문에 없다.
### lit40-hard-02-073 — skill text_structure_purpose · 유형 underlined_portion_function
[지문]
Cleotilde and Imtiaz had played chess in the abandoned orchard outside Lyon every Sunday since the club lost its hall. __Their board sat on a cut stump, and beneath it, on a card gone soft with damp, the club's oldest rule declared that a piece once touched must be moved.__ The pear trees had gone wild; fruit split in the grass and drew wasps. The two rivals spoke little, played slowly, and kept score in a notebook that neither would let the other hold. For eleven years the lead had passed between them like a coin. This Sunday a wasp settled on Imtiaz's queen. He flicked it off, and his knuckle tipped the queen onto its side. Moving her now would cost him the game and the lead. Cleotilde studied the fallen piece, then the stump. She drew out the card, folded it once, and put it in her coat. Then she stood the queen upright on her square and waited for him to play.

[질문] Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
A) It sets the scene by describing how the two rivals arrange their weekly game.
B) It presents a rule whose later setting aside reveals what Cleotilde values most.
C) It contrasts the club's orderly customs with the wild disorder of the orchard.
D) It suggests the rivals cling to old customs since losing the club's hall.

[표시된 정답] B
[해설]
밑줄 문장은 단독으로 보면 그루터기 위 체스판과 눅눅한 카드 한 장을 묘사하는 배경 설명처럼 보이고, 바로 뒤 문장은 무성한 과수원을 그려 대조처럼 읽히게 한다. 그러나 후반에 Imtiaz가 말벌을 쫓다 퀸을 건드려 규칙대로라면 경기와 선두를 잃게 되자, Cleotilde는 그 카드를 접어 넣고 퀸을 다시 세운 뒤 그의 수를 기다린다. 따라서 밑줄 문장은 나중에 규칙을 접어 두는 선택을 통해 그녀가 규칙보다 공정한 승부를 중시함을 드러내도록 기준을 미리 심어 둔 것이므로 B가 정답이다. A는 표면 기능만, C는 바로 뒤 문장과의 관계만 보았고, D는 지문의 '홀을 잃었다'는 표현을 빌려 일반화했다.
### lit40-hard-02-074 — skill text_structure_purpose · 유형 underlined_portion_function
[지문]

Her hands shook; twice the film slipped from the sprockets, and twice he said nothing. When the picture at last steadied on the screen, he took a marker from his pocket. On the strip of tape above the booth door, under his own name, he wrote a second one: Lara.

[질문] Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
A) It portrays Bogdan as an old friend who still mourns Larissa's grandmother.
B) It shifts the focus from family memories toward the daily work of the booth.
C) It introduces a name whose later use signals Larissa's new place in the booth.
D) It suggests that Larissa tolerates Bogdan's old habits mainly out of politeness.

[표시된 정답] C
[해설]
밑줄 문장은 단독으로 보면 Bogdan이 세상을 떠난 할머니를 그리워하며 옛 애칭을 쓰는 인물 묘사처럼 보인다. 그러나 후반에 Larissa가 처음 혼자 영사기를 걸어 화면을 안정시키자, Bogdan은 30년 동안 자기 이름만 있던 문 위 테이프에 바로 그 애칭을 적는다. 따라서 밑줄 문장은 그 이름이 나중에 영사실에서 그녀의 새 자리를 표시하는 데 쓰이도록 미리 심어 둔 장치이므로 C가 정답이다. A는 밑줄 문장의 표면만, B는 바로 뒤 영사실 묘사와의 관계만 보았고, D는 'she let him'을 빌려 일반화했을 뿐 후반 사건을 설명하지 못한다.
### lit40-hard-02-076 — skill text_structure_purpose · 유형 underlined_portion_function
[지문]
Aiko kept everything. In the harbor town in Hokkaido where we had both retired, her house held forty years of programs from the theater where we once sang duets, each pressed flat and labeled by year. __She told me once, over tea, that she had never missed a single performance of mine, not even after we stopped singing together.__ I laughed, and she poured more tea. Her husband, Haruo, mended nets on the jetty below the house and lifted a hand whenever I passed. Last winter, after Aiko's stroke, Haruo asked me to help him sort her desk. In the bottom drawer, beneath the programs, lay ticket stubs, one for every concert I had given alone, in Osaka, in Sendai, in cities she had sworn she had never seen. Haruo held one to the window light. He did not ask what it meant, and I returned the stubs to the order in which she had left them.

[질문] Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
A) It presents a remark that a later discovery shows to have been accurate.
B) It offers a polite compliment that the narrator takes as overstated.
C) It introduces the friendship that Haruo shares with the narrator in town.
D) It shows that Aiko kept old records mainly out of a love of order.

[표시된 정답] A
[해설]
밑줄 문장은 단독으로 보면 옛 동료의 인사치레이고, 화자도 웃어넘기며 차를 더 받는다. 그러나 후반에 서랍 속에서 화자가 혼자 연 모든 콘서트의 표가 나오고, 그중에는 Aiko가 가 본 적 없다고 했던 도시들도 있다. 따라서 밑줄 문장은 나중의 발견으로 말 그대로 사실이었음이 드러나는 말을 미리 심어 둔 것이므로 A가 정답이다. B는 화자의 웃음에 기대 표면 기능만 골랐고, C는 바로 뒤 Haruo 소개와의 관계만 보았으며, D는 'kept everything'을 빌려 일반화했을 뿐 서랍의 발견을 설명하지 못한다.
### lit40-hard-02-077 — skill central_ideas_details · 유형 narrator_attitude
[지문]
I keep my spice stall in the old galley of a ship that someone dragged ashore in Marrakesh, and Joaquin has been my worst customer for nine years. He haggles over cumin he has already decided to buy. He tells strangers that my scales lean toward the house. Last spring his nephew in Valencia offered him a room and a job minding a café, and Joaquin announced it to the whole galley as if I had lost a bet. I told him Valencia was finally getting someone to argue with. Hamza, he said, you will starve without my complaints. I was not worried, exactly. Still, I began weighing his cumin a little heavy, which he noticed and called theft in reverse. The week he was meant to leave, I did not take down the card above the stove that reads JOAQUIN'S STOOL, though I had threatened to for years. On the Thursday he came in anyway, his ticket folded in his shirt pocket, and I poured his tea before he finished complaining about the price.

[질문] Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Joaquin?
A) Mild relief at his departure while trading jokes about his complaints
B) Warm regard for him while feeling guilty about his claims of unfair scales
C) Quiet reluctance to lose him while treating his departure as a joke
D) Good-natured rivalry with him while expecting the café to suit him better

[표시된 정답] C
[해설]
앞부분에서 화자는 Joaquin을 '최악의 손님'이라 부르고 Valencia 이야기를 농담으로 받아치며 투덜대는 말투를 유지한다. 중간의 'not worried, exactly'라는 망설이는 정정 뒤에, 화자는 그의 커민을 몰래 넉넉히 달아 주고 떠날 주에도 그의 의자 표지를 떼지 않는 행동을 보인다. 이렇게 떨어진 두 행동은 말투와 달리 그를 잃고 싶지 않은 마음을 드러내므로 C가 정답이다. A는 농담조 말투만 읽었고, B는 애정의 이유를 저울에 대한 죄책감으로 바꾸었으며, D는 지문의 café·argue 표현을 빌려 경쟁 관계로 일반화했다.
### lit40-hard-02-079 — skill central_ideas_details · 유형 narrator_attitude
[지문]

her cane, her folding stool, and the rule we never made aloud.
Solange, retired from the bench, walks the dry bed of the river

too loose, too proud, inadmissible.

[질문] Which choice best describes the speaker's attitude toward Solange?
A) Watchful devotion to her while keeping up a show of weary teasing
B) Tired impatience with her while putting up with her rulings out of habit

My grandfather put down his spoon and asked me to say it again, slowly. He and Siti had not spoken in twenty years, for reasons no one at our table would name. The next morning he put on his good shirt, the one kept for funerals, and walked toward the school; my mother told the neighbors he had gone to the market. That week the upright piano in the music room stayed locked, and its key hung on a nail no one would touch. By the cool season the story had come to nothing, and Siti stayed. On Saturdays a satchel of sheet music began to appear on our hall bench, and from the kitchen I could hear two old players arguing over tempo, then starting the same bar again. Aung, my grandfather would call, bring the second chair.

[질문] Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
A) A boy repeats a rumor at dinner and sends his grandfather on a hidden errand.
B) Two old musicians take up playing together again after many years of silence.
C) A grandfather's long quarrel with a teacher gives rise to the rumor about her leaving.
D) A boy's careless repeating of gossip opens the way to a long-delayed reunion.

[표시된 정답] D
[해설]
앞부분에서 화자는 소문을 저녁 식탁에 옮기고, 할아버지는 20년간 말하지 않던 Siti를 위해 학교로 향한다. 중간의 잠긴 피아노는 설명 없이 남지만, 뒷부분에서 Siti의 악보 가방이 집에 나타나고 두 노인이 함께 연주한다. 두 사건을 연결하면 경솔하게 옮긴 소문이 오래된 관계 회복의 계기가 되었다는 D가 요지다. A는 사건 1만, B는 사건 2만 다루며, C는 소문과 불화의 인과 방향을 뒤집었다.
